sections.title: The 60-second business brief
sections.body:
Radio Mirchi is the radio and entertainment brand operated by ENIL. A local station brings listeners to its hosts and shows. Advertisers buy airtime, sponsored segments and city campaigns to reach that audience. S7

ENIL also reports on businesses such as Gaana. Its group revenue and profit include activities beyond radio. For station decisions, look at the city, the show, ad sales and repeat bookings. S1

sections.title: One morning in Delhi
sections.body:
Imagine Neha driving to work in Delhi. She turns on Radio Mirchi because she likes the presenter and the music. She hears a song, a conversation about the city and a short ad for a café opening near her office. She pays nothing to hear the show.

Now look at that same morning from the café owner’s side. He has tables to fill and a limited advertising budget. He chooses Mirchi because the café needs customers in Delhi. He books a 20-second message to run several mornings that week. Neha is the listener. The café is the paying customer. Mirchi earns money by broadcasting the message they agreed on. This café is an illustrative example.

At the end of the week, the owner has two questions. Did Mirchi play the ad as promised? The station can show him when it aired. Did it bring anyone through the door? A breakfast offer with a code mentioned on air can help him count some of those visits. His answer will influence whether he buys another week.

sections.title: What changes when the customer wants more than an ad?
sections.body:
Suppose the café wants people to taste its food. Hearing a breakfast ad and trying the breakfast are different experiences. The owner could ask Mirchi to organise a tasting with a local radio host. Now the work includes planning the gathering, arranging the host and telling listeners where to come. The café and Mirchi would agree a fee for that work.

The fee Mirchi earns is revenue. What it spends on the host, travel and production is a cost. What remains after those direct costs helps pay for running the station. This explains why a large event can bring in more money than a radio ad yet leave less after expenses.

At a ticketed event, a second kind of buyer appears. A runner buys admission to take part. A company may pay to have its name and activities at the run. That company is a sponsor. How much of the ticket money Mirchi keeps depends on its agreement with the organiser.

sections.title: Four real stories: what did the client need Mirchi to do?
sections.body:
A car, a home appliance, a tin of paint and an insurance policy are bought in different ways. That is why these four companies used Mirchi differently. ENIL, the company that operates Radio Mirchi, described the work in its report for April 2024 to March 2025.

MG Hector took the radio host to the showroom. Think about buying a car. An ad can help you remember the name, but you will probably want to sit in the car and drive it. Mirchi hosts took part in showroom test drives and talked about the car’s features with participants. For the showroom manager, the next question is simple: how many people who tried the car came back to discuss buying one?

Xiaomi took its products to people’s homes. Instead of waiting for families to visit an electronics store, its Smart Home League brought demonstrations and challenges to ten residential communities. Residents could see the products in use. Posts about the activity were displayed more than a million times, according to ENIL. That tells Xiaomi how widely the posts appeared. To learn what residents bought afterwards, it would also need sales records.

Dulux made the paint shops the centre of the story. Dulux sells through dealers: shop owners who stock its paint. It ran a display contest involving 20 selected dealers across five cities. Mirchi hosts visited shops, and entries were featured on radio and online. The people Dulux wanted to involve first were the shop owners themselves. A shop could earn recognition for a good display, and Dulux could give its products a more prominent place in the store.

ACKO met people at a run. Insurance is usually something people think about when they need a policy. ACKO also appeared in neighbourhood activities and a Neon Run across five cities. The run gave people an enjoyable occasion to encounter the brand. A runner attending, remembering ACKO and later buying a policy are three different outcomes. The report describes the event and leaves the sales outcome open.

These are examples of work delivered. The report gives no fee or profit for each client. ENIL FY25 annual report, pages 15 and 16

One number in plain English. For July to September 2026, ENIL said radio generated 53% of its Indian revenue. Imagine all the money its Indian businesses earned in that quarter as ₹100. About ₹53 came from radio. The figure describes revenue before costs. S2

sections.title: How are ENIL, Mirchi and Gaana connected?
sections.body:
ENIL is the company. Mirchi is its radio and entertainment brand. Gaana is its music streaming service.

ENIL stands for Entertainment Network (India) Limited. It belongs to the wider Times Group and publishes its own financial results. When you quote revenue in the interview, say “ENIL reported…” and give the period. S6 S2

Who pays whom? Imagine a Delhi café buying an ad on a Mirchi morning show. The café pays to reach listeners. A Gaana subscriber pays to listen to music. Both activities sit within ENIL’s business, but they earn money in different ways. S7 S5

Where do Mirchi Plus and Mirchi Live fit? Mirchi Plus is a name readers may see on digital content and app listings. Mirchi Live is where people can find events and campaigns such as Mirchi Freshers. S20 S12

A useful city personality understands language, humour, neighbourhoods and cultural timing. Treat that relationship as a product asset, with editorial judgment and talent continuity.

sections.title: The radio equation
sections.body:
Model

Net Revenue from paid radio ad time = ad seconds available × percentage of ad time sold × actual revenue per second. Use the same city, time of day and time period for every input.

A 5% price reduction needs more than 5% additional sold volume to keep revenue unchanged: 1 ÷ 0.95 − 1 = 5.26%. If capacity or listener ad tolerance is already constrained, the extra volume may not be achievable. Discounting should be evaluated against total profit after direct costs, advertiser retention and future pricing expectations.

Percentage of ad time sold and price are not independent. Prime time, local festivals, premium sponsorships and bundled contracts alter the inventory mix. A national average can hide both healthy cities and weak stations.

sections.title: Questions that prevent misleading revenue stories
sections.body:
• Is ticket revenue shown gross or net of platform fees, taxes and organiser share?
  • Is an event owned, co-produced, commissioned or only promoted? Branding alone does not establish IP ownership.
  • Do digital solutions include media purchased on behalf of clients? Separate billings from retained margin.
  • When is sponsorship cash collected versus recorded as revenue?
  • Does a bundle pay Gaana on shipment, activation or usage? What is the effective net consideration?
  • Are sold to existing customers revenues extra or shifted from another Mirchi budget?

sections.body:
A useful radio proposition combines music with familiar personalities, local context, timely information and participation. The commercial product is access to that relationship. A listener who enjoys an RJ is not automatically a digital user or a ticket buyer; every handoff still has to earn the next action.

sections.title: Proposed pilot: a local advertiser return loop
sections.body:
Analysis

Customer need

A local business needs a credible way to bring relevant people to a store or offer, and an easy way to decide whether to buy another campaign. It may have neither a marketing analyst nor a full agency.

Analysis

Minimum product

Create a scoped campaign brief, a verified landing page or call response mechanism, a delivery log and a concise close-out report. Sell a bounded test before automating the entire sales process.

Analysis

Validation

Select a small, comparable advertiser user group; predefine one primary outcome. Use matched stores or time/geographic comparison groups that do not receive the change when practical. Report uncertainty, not just attributed clicks.

Success criterion to agree before launch: higher extra profit after direct costs from repeat advertisers with acceptable collection days, no rise in delivery exceptions and no deterioration in listener experience.

sections.title: Rights and regulatory dependencies
sections.body:
FM broadcast, online streaming, podcasts, social clips and event music can have different rights and contract conditions. Obtain a rights review for each intended reuse rather than treating a broadcast licence as permission for every platform.

The government’s 2024 expansion announcement sets a 4% annual licence fee for the specified new-city channels. This must not be assumed to replace all existing ENIL licence obligations. S28

In an interview, ask how renewal exposure and regulatory changes enter deciding where to invest money. Treat potential reforms as scenarios, not approved future savings.

sections.title: Know the frequency, but check the city
sections.body:
The September MIB list includes Mirchi at 98.3 MHz in Delhi, and at both 98.3 and 95 MHz in Bengaluru. Frequencies and brand variants vary by market; “98.3” is not the complete network map. S35

Before discussing a particular city, verify the current station, format, listener proposition and advertiser set. A second frequency should be evaluated on audience and commercial differentiation rather than assumed to be duplicate reach.

sections.title: The attendee journey is the retention product
sections.body:
• Discover: relevant city, format, date, artist and accessible information; explain why this event fits the person.
  • Decide: show total price, inclusions, age/access rules, transport information and cancellation terms before checkout.
  • Attend: ticket retrieval, entry throughput, clear help, safe capacity, water and medical support.
  • Remember: useful post-event content and feedback; obtain permission for future contact.
  • Return: recommend the next relevant event, not every event nationwide. Reward repeat attendance only when extra margin pays for the benefit.

sections.title: Proposed event growth system
sections.body:
Start with one repeatable format in two contrasting cities. Give every edition a signed sponsor plan, a downside Income and cost sheet, a cash exposure ceiling and an attendee service plan. Link the promotion source to a first-party or partner-compliant event record so the team can understand conversion without double-counting.

Analysis

Before go / no-go

Secure minimum sponsorship and venue options. Track break-even paid admissions against realistic demand, then set spend-release gates.

Analysis

During execution

Use one operating checklist with named owners. Escalate queues, safety, artist delays and fulfilment gaps quickly. Capture only the data necessary for the intended service.

Analysis

After the edition

Close collections, vendor settlements and sponsor fulfilment. Compare actual profit after direct costs with the quote and track sponsor / attendee return over subsequent editions.

sections.title: Discovery plan with evidence standards
sections.body:
Analysis

Qualitative

Interview customers who completed the job and those who abandoned it. Observe the task rather than asking which feature they want. Recruit beyond vocal fans and recent complainants.

Analysis

Quantitative

Validate event and account identity, payment outcomes and instrumentation before using funnels. Segment by channel and release version so a rollout does not look like a behavioural trend.

Analysis

Decision

Write the evidence that would change the proposed priority. A hypothesis should be easy to reject when research shows the need is small, already met or too costly to serve.

Offer a limited catalogue by objective, city and budget, supported by a clear delivery plan and response measurement. Start with a category that repeats frequently enough to evaluate within a practical window. A sales-assisted workflow is a reasonable first version; self-service comes after the offer is repeatable.

  • Primary: extra 90-day advertiser profit after direct costs and repeat booking.
  • Checks that protect service and profit: collection days, deal discount, delivery exceptions, sales time and listener experience.
  • Evidence: matched accounts or a phased rollout; track displaced radio or solution spend.
  • Stop: higher gross billings with lower retained margin or longer credit exposure.

sections.body:
Put event discovery, booking partners, sponsor fulfilment and the edition Income and cost sheet into one operating view. Preserve attendee consent and ticket-platform contractual boundaries. The product should support a faster, better proceed or stop decision, not merely make another listing page.

  • Primary: actual edition profit after direct costs and cash conversion.
  • Customer: entry wait, issue resolution, sponsor fulfilment and subsequent return.
  • Scale: comparable editions meet economics and service gates across cities.
  • Stop: the model depends on uncontracted sponsorship, unrealistic attendance or unsustainable local workload.

sections.body:
For content continuity, start with one franchise and preserve the destination from social post to story page to app. For AI, observe a real workflow first: transcription, clip selection, tagging, local adaptation or campaign report assembly may be candidates. Compare turnaround and error rate against the current process.

Quality and rights are part of the product

Keep editorial review, talent permission, licensed-use boundaries and factual checks in the release criteria. A faster output is valuable only if it is usable and creates no extra correction or rights burden.

pages.label: How to measure success
pages.title: How to tell whether the changes are working.
pages.desc: The measures to track for radio, events, subscriptions and brand campaigns, with simple definitions.

sections.title: The main measures and what drives them
sections.body:
BusinessOutcomeLeading measuresChecks that protect service and profit
RadioProfit after direct costs from retained advertisersActual price earned, percentage of ad time sold, repeat spend, delivery.Ad load, discount leakage, credit days, make-goods.
EventsActual edition profit after direct costs and cash recoveryPaid attendance, actual income per ticket after deductions, sponsor collections, repeat intent.Safety, entry wait, refunds, vendor exposure, fulfilment.
GaanaProfit from subscribers who stayIntent-to-play, paid access success, retained listening days, renewal user groups.Playback reliability, support cost, refunds, partner economics.
Digital solutionsProfit kept after delivery costs per clientProposal speed, win rate, repeat scope, on-time delivery.Pass-through spend, rework, collections and concentration.
ContentUseful retained audience and attributable commercial valueRepeat consumption, series completion, qualified handoffs.Rights, quality, creator workload and platform dependence.

A proposed shared lens is extra profit after direct costs from repeat customer relationships. It needs a business-specific definition; a sponsor, an advertiser and a subscriber cannot share one base number.

sections.title: Definitions that need to be explicit
sections.body:
• Activation: a successful value moment, not an install or a login. Define the required listening or campaign outcome before measurement.
  • Retention: the fraction of a starting user group that meets the defined value event in a later window. Keep trial, partner and paid user groups separate.
  • Profit after direct costs: net recorded revenue minus the costs included in the agreed cost breakdown. State which variable, direct and allocated costs are included.
  • Extra results caused by the change: the change versus a credible estimate of what would have happened without the change, not the number of people with a campaign tag.
  • Repeat event customer: one person attending a second relevant edition, counted once using information they have permitted us to link.
  • Actual price earned: actual revenue after discounts and the adjustments agreed with finance.

sections.title: The important rates, with simple formulas
sections.body:
MeasureHow to calculate itWhat to keep consistent
First-play conversionPeople with a successful first play ÷ eligible people who entered the journey × 100.Use people, not a mixture of visits, installs and accounts. Define a successful play.
7-day / 30-day returnPeople from the starting group who listen in the chosen later window ÷ people in that starting group × 100.State whether you mean exactly day 7, any day in week 2, or a rolling window.
Episode completionEligible episode starts that reach the agreed completion point ÷ eligible starts × 100.State the completion threshold; report episode length and repeated starts separately.
Paid renewalSubscriptions that renew successfully ÷ subscriptions due to renew in the period × 100.Separate annual, monthly, trial and partner plans. A cancelled future renewal is not always immediate loss of access.
Revenue per paying userSubscription revenue for a period ÷ the agreed average number of paying users in that period.State monthly or annual, exclude or include taxes consistently, and separate paying from active users.
Customer acquisition costIncluded marketing, partner and incentive spend ÷ new paying customers from that spend.A device shipped or a free trial started is not a paying customer.
Radio ad-time soldAd seconds sold ÷ ad seconds available for sale × 100.Compare the same city, station, time of day and period.
Radio price earnedRecorded ad revenue after agreed adjustments ÷ ad seconds sold.Use the same treatment of agency fees, discounts and bundles.
Advertiser repeat rateAdvertisers who buy again in the chosen window ÷ advertisers eligible to buy again × 100.Also measure repeat spend and profit: one small repeat order can hide lost budget.
Booking conversionCompleted paid bookings ÷ eligible booking journeys started × 100.Track people, orders and tickets separately; a couple ticket is not one attendee.
Paid attendancePaid-ticket holders who enter ÷ valid paid-ticket holders expected × 100.Separate complimentary passes, refunds, no-shows and capacity.
Sponsor renewalEligible sponsors who book the next comparable edition ÷ eligible sponsors × 100.Also compare retained sponsorship value, cash collected and delivery costs.
Event direct profitSponsor income + ticket income after deductions + other contracted income − included event delivery costs.List the included costs. Direct profit is not the same as final company profit.
AI usable-output rateAI outputs accepted after the agreed review ÷ outputs reviewed × 100.Include review time, correction time, rights checks and serious errors when judging value.

sections.title: Three experiments worth designing properly
sections.body:
ExperimentPrimary testDesign caution
Partner activation journeyExtra profit from users who keep returning per eligible user group.Randomise or phase within comparable partner user groups; preserve offer and season.
Advertiser package90-day repeat profit after direct costs versus current offer.Account for sales selection, account size and spending shifted from an existing offer.
Event reminder / return loopExtra net ticket profit after direct costs from permitted audience.Use a comparison group that does not receive the change; include discount cost, refunds and substitution between events.

Choose sample size from the actual starting result, the smallest improvement worth detecting, allocation and desired statistical precision. No sample-size number is invented here. Predefine the decision window and checks that protect service and profit, and avoid repeatedly stopping the test at the first positive result.

sections.title: How to measure results across offline and online
sections.body:
On-air codes, tagged links, unique landing pages, booking references and matching customer records can identify observed response. They do not automatically capture all radio exposure or establish causation. Pair response tracking with comparison groups that do not receive the change or matched comparisons where feasible, and report uncertainty.

The stakeholder-friendly dashboard

Show what was delivered, what people did, what changed versus the comparison and how much profit after direct costs remained. Keep these four layers separate so a reach metric does not quietly become a revenue claim.

pages.label: Try the numbers
pages.title: Try the numbers: events, subscriptions and radio ads.
pages.desc: Change the example inputs to see income, direct costs, profit and the point where the costs are covered. These are illustrations.

sections.title: Event edition: profit after direct costs and break-even
sections.body:
All amounts are in rupees, excluding GST. Ticket price is net organiser receipt; no fees or taxes are deducted again. Variable cost is per paid attendee. Sponsorship and ancillary income must be contracted; allocated corporate overhead is excluded.

Formula: profit after direct costs = paid attendees × (net ticket receipt − variable cost) + sponsorship + ancillary − fixed costs. Break-even attendees = ceiling(max(0, fixed − sponsorship − ancillary) ÷ ticket profit after direct costs), subject to positive ticket profit after direct costs and capacity.

sections.title: Subscriber group: first-year profit after direct costs
sections.body:
This model starts with paying users. It is not suitable for treating a complimentary hardware bundle as full-price revenue. Annual price below is net recorded service revenue per paid year, excluding taxes. Cost-share and retention inputs are hypothetical, not Gaana disclosures.

Formula: annual unit profit after direct costs before acquisition = annual net revenue × (1 − variable cost share) − annual service cost. First-year user group profit after direct costs subtracts acquisition spend. Renewal illustration applies the same revenue and costs for each customer to renewing users, excludes new acquisition and is not lifetime value.

sections.title: Radio: percentage of ad time sold versus price
sections.body:
An illustrative period with a fixed pool of available ad seconds. Changing utilisation and price earned does not account for changes in station, time of day, inventory quality, collections or extra operating costs.

Decision rule

A revenue increase does not establish a profit increase. Use these models to expose assumptions, then add the actual cost, cash and customer constraints before recommending a decision.
